abstract: BackgroundWhether discontinuing statin therapy in older adults with at least two chronic conditions but no known cardiovascular disease affects the time to a first cardiovascular event is not well characterized. MethodsWe conducted an international, open-label, randomized, controlled trial that enrolled adults at least 70 years of age who were taking statins for primary prevention. Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either discontinue or continue statin therapy and other lipid-lowering therapies. The primary outcome was a composite of nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal ischemic stroke, or death from any cause, whichever occurred first. The primary analysis assessed noninferiority on the basis of the between-group difference in restricted mean event-free survival time at 2 years, with a noninferiority margin of −5.2 weeks. ResultsA total of 1880 participants underwent randomization: 938 were assigned to the discontinuation group and 942 to the continuation group. The mean age of the participants was 77.5 years, and 46.9% were women. The between-group difference in the restricted mean event-free survival time at 2 years was −2.0 weeks (95% confidence interval, −3.7 to −0.3; P<0.001 for noninferiority). Over a median follow-up of 103 weeks, 119 participants (12.7%) in the discontinuation group and 87 (9.2%) in the continuation group had a primary-outcome event. At least one serious adverse event occurred in 43.0% of the participants in the discontinuation group and in 39.8% in the continuation group. ConclusionsAmong older adults with at least two chronic conditions but no known cardiovascular disease, discontinuation of statin therapy was noninferior to continuation with respect to major cardiovascular events or death from any cause at 2 years. (Funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation; STREAM ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05178420.)
title: Discontinuing Statins in Older Adults without Cardiovascular Disease

abstract: Background: The efficacy and safety of retatrutide, an investigational triple agonist of glucosedependent insulinotropic polypeptide, glucagon-like peptide 1, and glucagon receptors for painful knee osteoarthritis (OA) in people with obesity are unknown.Methods: Two phase 3 trials enrolled adults with painful knee OA and BMI ≥27 kg/m 2 without diabetes.Participants were randomly assigned to once-weekly subcutaneous retatrutide (TRIUMPH-4, N=445: 9-mg, 12-mg; TRIUMPH-1-OA, N=574: 4-mg, 9-mg, 12-mg) or placebo.TRIUMPH-4 co-primary endpoints were change in WOMAC pain score (range, 0-10, higher=more pain) and percent change in bodyweight at week 68; TRIUMPH-1-OA primary endpoint was change in WOMAC pain score at week 80.For non-pain-related endpoints, intercurrent events were handled by a treatment policy strategy (treatment-regimen estimand [TRE]).For pain-related outcomes, a hybrid-treatment estimand was applied with a hypothetical strategy for participants with intercurrent events suggesting treatment failure and treatment policy strategy elsewhere.We also report an intention-to-treat estimand that applied a treatment policy strategy for all intercurrent events (hereafter ITT).Results: In TRIUMPH-4 (68 weeks), mean change in WOMAC pain (hybrid-treatment estimand) was -3.96 (9-mg), -3.74 (12-mg) and -2.12 (placebo) (difference vs. placebo [95% CI] -1.83 [-2.37,-1.30],-1.61 [-2.16,-1.07],respectively); differences by ITT estimand: -1.70 [-2.19,-1.22];-1.38 [-1.91,-0.85])(P <0.001).Mean percent change in bodyweight was -20.0%(9-mg), -23.7% (12-mg) and -4.6% (placebo) (differences: -15.4 [-18.7,-12.1];-19.2 [-22.4,-15.9])(P <0.001).In TRIUMPH-1-OA (80 weeks), mean change in WOMAC pain (hybrid-treatment estimand) was -3.22 (4-mg), -3.48 (9-mg), -3.64 (12-mg) and -1.87 (placebo) (differences: -1.35 [-1.92,-0.78];-1.61 [-2.20,-1.02];-1.77 [-2.34,-1.20]);and differences by ITT estimand: -0.96 [-1.61,-0.30];-1.41 [-2.07,-0.75];-1.64 [-2.26,-1.02])(P≤0.005).In both trials, serious adverse events (AEs) were more common with retatrutide than placebo, and gastrointestinal AEs were most common.Conclusions: In participants with painful knee OA and obesity, retatrutide treatment resulted in significant reductions in both WOMAC pain scores and bodyweight.(Funded by Eli Lilly and Company; TRIUMPH-4 ClinicalTrials.gov:NCT05931367; TRIUMPH-1 ClinicalTrials.gov:NCT05929066) Osteoarthritis (OA), a progressive joint disease, often includes pain that limits quality of life and confers substantial socioeconomic burdens on patients, healthcare systems, and society.[1][2][3] Obesity is a risk factor in both OA onset and progression.[1][2][3] Excess bodyweight increases mechanical loading on weight-bearing joints; further, increased joint stress accelerates cartilage degeneration and possible malalignment.1,3,4 Excess adiposity may also contribute to a systemic, low-grade inflammatory state.5 Weight reduction is considered an important component of knee OA management; each pound of bodyweight lost is associated with an approximately 4-fold load reduction across the knee.6 Biomechanical and clinical benefits increase with weight loss; progressively greater weight reduction is associated with lower maximum knee compressive forces and greater symptom improvements.7 Clinical guidelines include weight reduction alongside exercise, pharmacologic therapies such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents, intra-articular injections, and surgical interventions.8,9 Current pharmacologic therapies may provide modest efficacy but limited tolerability and safety.A study of semaglutide suggested improved knee OA pain, 10 highlighting the possibility that additional obesity therapeutics might address both excess bodyweight and knee OA symptoms.Retatrutide is an investigational triple-receptor agonist of the glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), and glucagon receptors.In phase 2 clinical trials in patients with obesity, retatrutide demonstrated average weight reductions from 8.7%-24.2%,versus 2.1% with placebo (percentage point difference: -6.6 to -22.1), at 48 weeks.11 The two trials presented here, one published in part previously, 12 evaluated the efficacy, tolerability, and safety of once-weekly injectable retatrutide in adults with painful knee OA and obesity.
title: Retatrutide Once Weekly in Adults with Knee Osteoarthritis Pain and Obesity

abstract: BackgroundUncertainty persists regarding the effects of intensive blood-pressure lowering in patients with type 2 diabetes. MethodsIn this multicenter, open-label, randomized trial conducted in Brazil, patients with elevated blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, and high cardiovascular risk received intensive therapy targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 120 mm Hg or standard therapy targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 140 mm Hg. The primary end point was a composite of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or hospitalization for unstable angina or heart failure. ResultsOf the 9476 ethnically diverse patients who were enrolled, 4745 were assigned to receive intensive therapy and 4731 to receive standard therapy. The mean (±SD) age was 64.7±8.2 years, and 5871 of the patients (62.0%) were women. The mean systolic blood pressure during follow-up (with exclusion of the first 3 months) was 121.8±10.8 mm Hg in the intensive-therapy group and 135.4±8.2 mm Hg in the standard-therapy group. During a median follow-up of 4.0 years (interquartile range, 3.9 to 4.0), a primary-outcome event occurred in 286 patients (6.0%; 1.65 events per 100 person-years) in the intensive-therapy group and in 315 patients (6.7%; 1.83 events per 100 person-years) in the standard-therapy group (hazard ratio, 0.90; 95% confidence interval, 0.77 to 1.06; P=0.20). Serious adverse events occurred in 706 patients (14.9%) with intensive therapy and in 693 patients (14.6%) with standard therapy. ConclusionsAmong patients with type 2 diabetes, targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 120 mm Hg, as compared with less than 140 mm Hg, did not reduce the occurrence of major cardiovascular events. (Funded by Hospital Israelita Albert Einstein and the Brazilian Ministry of Health; OPTIMAL-DIABETES ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04040634.)
title: Intensive Blood-Pressure Lowering in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes

abstract: BackgroundWhether intensive blood-pressure control reduces cardiovascular risk after cerebrovascular events remains uncertain. MethodsIn this multicenter, open-label, randomized trial conducted at 30 sites in Brazil, we assigned participants with elevated blood pressure and previous ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack to receive intensive treatment targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 120 mm Hg or to receive standard treatment targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 140 mm Hg. The primary outcome was a composite of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or hospitalization for unstable angina or heart failure. ResultsA total of 4368 participants were enrolled, with 2172 assigned to intensive treatment and 2196 to standard treatment. The mean (±SD) age of the participants was 63.9±11.2 years, and 2093 (47.9%) were women. During the follow-up period, excluding the first 3 months, the mean systolic blood pressure was 122.0±11.5 mm Hg (median, 119.6 mm Hg) in the intensive-treatment group and 135.2±9.7 mm Hg (median, 135.0 mm Hg) in the standard-treatment group, with a between-group mean difference of 13.1 mm Hg (95% confidence interval [CI], 12.5 to 13.8). Over a median follow-up of 3.9 years, a primary-outcome event occurred in 236 participants (10.9%; 3.25 events per 100 person-years) with intensive treatment and in 297 (13.5%; 4.11 events per 100 person-years) with standard treatment (hazard ratio, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.67 to 0.94; P=0.007). The composite renal outcome (sustained reduction of ≥50% in the estimated glomerular filtration rate or progression to end-stage renal disease) was more common with intensive treatment. The overall incidence of serious adverse events was similar in the two groups. ConclusionsAmong participants with previous ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack, targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 120 mm Hg resulted in a lower incidence of major cardiovascular events than targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 140 mm Hg. (Funded by Hospital Israelita Albert Einstein and the Brazilian Ministry of Health; OPTIMAL-STROKE ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04036409.)
title: Intensive Blood-Pressure Control in Patients with Previous Ischemic Stroke

abstract: The melting temperature and electrical resistivity of iron at high pressure are essential for understanding Earth’s core. Here we use a new high-pressure method – microsecond pulsed Joule heating in diamond anvil cells – to identify melting and measure resistivity of solid and liquid iron. More than 300 reproducible melting measurements indicate a surprisingly shallow melting curve, reaching 6 K/GPa and 4160 ± 80 K at 200 GPa. Extrapolating in pressure and iron alloy composition, and combining with our 76 μ Ω cm measurement of liquid iron’s resistivity, we infer a relatively cold core-mantle boundary (3430 K) with a low adiabatic outer core heat flow (9.8 TW). This suggests thermal convection alone could have powered the geodynamo prior to inner core formation and that today’s lowermost mantle is fully solid.
title: Melting and resistivity of iron at Earth core conditions using pulsed Joule heating
